chapter: Writing, Oklahoma roots and the origins of bebop
title: 'Mop-Mop', 'I Got Rhythm' and harmony after 'How High the Moon'
summary: New lines on old changes, and the success of 'How High the Moon' changing harmony.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I know some people have said that Hawk got credit for writing "Mop-Mop," but it was really a figure that Charlie Parker played. I don't know.

Well, I don't know whether Charlie played that particular thing. I don't even know whether Hawk put it out. All I know is that when I came to New York they were playing it. So I don't know who wrote it, or who thought about the idea. But I know that everybody was playing it. I thought that it sounded like Prez to me, but I guess it wasn't -- I don't know. Maybe it was, I don't
Again, though, it sounded like a drum figure or a rhythmic figure.
Right. It just sounded like a rhythmic figure that was placed on "I Got Rhythm" or something.
Then, of course, there was the harmonic structure which changed so much in those years, and led to...

Yeah. But "Mop-Mop" was just "I Got Rhythm" except for the release, which went to... But it still had the same changes in the release. But it was just one of those things that, you know, it caught on because it said "mop-mop."
But I'm talking in general now. We were talking about the rhythmic influence on the music. But then to talk about how it changed harmonically.

Well, the harmonics really started changing after "How High The Moon" got a little bit of acclaim. Not a little bit; I mean a rather large amount of acclaim -- "How High The Moon." Because the changes just laid right. I mean, it wasn't that the tune was so pretty or anything, but they were easy to play in and they laid just about right. All the things dissolved right back into the other, and then we came right back to where you were to start off with on the chord change structure. But what can you say?
It just turned out all right.
Well, the practice of writing new lines on top of changes, of course, went back long before Bebop.
Yeah. Hell, that was still being done a long time ago.
But it seemed to be really emphasized in this period where people were really writing not just riff tunes off chord patterns, but really constructing intricate new melodies.

New melodies and everything. Yeah, that was the idea, was to keep really progressing with your ideas and your thoughts, and make them dissolve into what was being played, and not only rhythmic-wise, but just being able to play, and play all kinds of figures on any kind of a rhythmic melody. I mean, 'I Got Rhythm' was the same thing as 'Mop-Mop,' except that the figure of harmonics went up instead of staying on the same letter. [SINGS COMPARISON] Same thing all over, but it's just... Everybody has different ideas about how to play on the same idea.
